title: Immunology
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 400L Biology/Zoology department Immunology curriculum, building on 200/300L cell biology and microbiology: innate and adaptive immunity, cells and organs of the immune system, antibody structure and diversity, complement, MHC and antigen presentation, hypersensitivity, immune tolerance, vaccines, and immunodeficiency.

questions.question: Which of the following is a defining feature that distinguishes adaptive (acquired) immunity from innate immunity?
options: It acts immediately upon first exposure to a pathogen
It exhibits specificity for particular antigens and immunological memory on re-exposure
It uses only physical barriers such as skin and mucus
It does not involve any white blood cells
questions.correct_answer: It exhibits specificity for particular antigens and immunological memory on re-exposure
questions.explanation: Adaptive immunity is characterised by antigen specificity and immunological memory, allowing a faster, stronger secondary response, unlike the rapid but non-specific innate response.

questions.question: Which cell type is considered the most efficient professional antigen-presenting cell (APC) for initiating primary T-cell responses?
options: Erythrocytes
Dendritic cells
Platelets
Mast cells
questions.correct_answer: Dendritic cells
questions.explanation: Dendritic cells are the most potent professional APCs, capturing antigen in peripheral tissues and migrating to lymph nodes to prime naive T lymphocytes.

questions.question: Natural killer (NK) cells are important components of innate immunity because they:
options: Require prior sensitisation to a specific antigen before they can kill target cells
Recognise and kill virus-infected or tumour cells that have downregulated MHC class I expression, without prior sensitisation
Produce antibodies against pathogens
Present antigen on MHC class II to helper T cells
questions.correct_answer: Recognise and kill virus-infected or tumour cells that have downregulated MHC class I expression, without prior sensitisation
questions.explanation: NK cells are innate lymphocytes that kill cells lacking normal 'self' MHC class I ('missing self' hypothesis), providing immune surveillance without needing prior antigen-specific sensitisation.

questions.question: Which immunoglobulin class is the predominant antibody found in mucosal secretions such as saliva, tears, and breast milk?
options: IgG
IgM
IgA
IgE
questions.correct_answer: IgA
questions.explanation: Secretory IgA (usually as a dimer with a secretory component) is the major immunoglobulin in mucosal secretions, providing localised mucosal immunity.

questions.question: Which immunoglobulin class is the first to be produced during a primary immune response and exists as a pentamer in serum?
options: IgG
IgM
IgD
IgA
questions.correct_answer: IgM
questions.explanation: IgM is the first antibody class produced in a primary response; its pentameric structure (with the J chain) gives it high avidity, useful for early, relatively low-affinity antigen binding.

questions.question: Which immunoglobulin class is responsible for mediating type I (immediate) hypersensitivity reactions by binding to Fc receptors on mast cells and basophils?
options: IgG
IgE
IgA
IgM
questions.correct_answer: IgE
questions.explanation: IgE binds high-affinity Fc-epsilon receptors on mast cells and basophils; cross-linking of bound IgE by allergen triggers degranulation and release of histamine, mediating immediate hypersensitivity (allergic) reactions.

questions.question: The basic structural unit of an immunoglobulin (antibody) molecule consists of:
options: One heavy chain and one light chain only
Two identical heavy chains and two identical light chains linked by disulfide bonds
Four identical heavy chains
A single polypeptide chain with no disulfide bonds
questions.correct_answer: Two identical heavy chains and two identical light chains linked by disulfide bonds
questions.explanation: The basic Y-shaped immunoglobulin monomer is composed of two identical heavy (H) chains and two identical light (L) chains, held together by interchain disulfide bonds.

questions.question: The Fab region of an antibody molecule is primarily responsible for:
options: Binding to complement and Fc receptors on effector cells
Antigen binding, via its variable regions
Determining the antibody's isotype class switching
Crossing the placenta
questions.correct_answer: Antigen binding, via its variable regions
questions.explanation: The Fab (fragment antigen-binding) region, comprising the light chain and the VH-CH1 portion of the heavy chain, contains the variable regions that form the antigen-binding site.

questions.question: The generation of antibody diversity in developing B lymphocytes primarily depends on:
options: Random point mutations occurring only after antigen exposure
Somatic recombination of V, D, and J gene segments to assemble a functional immunoglobulin variable region gene
Horizontal gene transfer from pathogens
Alternative splicing of a single fixed variable region gene
questions.correct_answer: Somatic recombination of V, D, and J gene segments to assemble a functional immunoglobulin variable region gene
questions.explanation: V(D)J recombination, mediated by RAG1/RAG2 recombinases, randomly joins variable (V), diversity (D, heavy chain only), and joining (J) gene segments during B-cell development, generating vast antibody diversity.

questions.question: Somatic hypermutation, which further refines antibody affinity during a germinal centre response, introduces point mutations primarily into which region of the immunoglobulin gene?
options: The constant region only
The variable region, particularly the complementarity-determining regions (CDRs)
The signal peptide sequence
Intronic sequences unrelated to antigen binding
questions.correct_answer: The variable region, particularly the complementarity-determining regions (CDRs)
questions.explanation: Somatic hypermutation, driven by activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID), introduces point mutations concentrated in the variable region CDRs, allowing affinity maturation through selection of higher-affinity B cell clones.

questions.question: Class switch recombination allows a B cell to change the isotype of antibody it produces (e.g. from IgM to IgG) while:
options: Changing its antigen specificity at the same time
Retaining the same antigen-binding variable region, so specificity for the original antigen is preserved
Losing all antigen specificity permanently
Only occurring in T lymphocytes
questions.correct_answer: Retaining the same antigen-binding variable region, so specificity for the original antigen is preserved
questions.explanation: Class switch recombination changes the constant region (and thus effector function/isotype) of the antibody heavy chain while leaving the rearranged variable region, and hence antigen specificity, unchanged.

questions.question: MHC class I molecules present antigenic peptides primarily derived from which pathway?
options: Exogenous antigens phagocytosed from the extracellular space
Endogenous (cytosolic) antigens, such as viral proteins synthesised within the infected cell
Lipid antigens exclusively
Antigens absorbed directly from the gut
questions.correct_answer: Endogenous (cytosolic) antigens, such as viral proteins synthesised within the infected cell
questions.explanation: MHC class I presents peptides derived from cytosolic/endogenous proteins (degraded by the proteasome, transported via TAP into the ER), signalling to CD8+ cytotoxic T cells that a cell is infected or abnormal.

questions.question: MHC class II molecules, which present exogenous antigen to CD4+ helper T cells, are expressed constitutively on which cell types?
options: All nucleated cells in the body
Professional antigen-presenting cells: dendritic cells, macrophages, and B lymphocytes
Only red blood cells
Only skeletal muscle cells
questions.correct_answer: Professional antigen-presenting cells: dendritic cells, macrophages, and B lymphocytes
questions.explanation: Unlike MHC class I (expressed on nearly all nucleated cells), MHC class II is constitutively expressed mainly on professional APCs -- dendritic cells, macrophages, and B cells -- to present exogenous antigen to CD4+ T helper cells.

questions.question: The CD8 co-receptor on cytotoxic T lymphocytes functions by:
options: Binding directly to MHC class II molecules
Binding to a conserved region of MHC class I molecules, stabilising the interaction between the T-cell receptor and peptide-MHC I complex
Acting as the primary antigen receptor itself
Secreting antibodies
questions.correct_answer: Binding to a conserved region of MHC class I molecules, stabilising the interaction between the T-cell receptor and peptide-MHC I complex
questions.explanation: CD8 is a co-receptor that binds the alpha-3 domain of MHC class I, stabilising TCR engagement and contributing to signal transduction, restricting CD8+ T cells to recognising antigen presented on MHC class I.

questions.question: Full activation of a naive T lymphocyte generally requires two signals: recognition of peptide-MHC by the T-cell receptor (signal 1) and which second signal?
options: Binding of complement C3b to the T cell
A co-stimulatory signal, e.g. CD28 on the T cell binding B7 (CD80/CD86) on the antigen-presenting cell
Direct contact with a pathogen's cell wall
Secretion of histamine by mast cells
questions.correct_answer: A co-stimulatory signal, e.g. CD28 on the T cell binding B7 (CD80/CD86) on the antigen-presenting cell
questions.explanation: The two-signal model of T-cell activation requires TCR-peptide-MHC recognition (signal 1) plus a co-stimulatory signal, classically CD28-B7 engagement (signal 2); absence of signal 2 can induce anergy.

questions.question: Regulatory T cells (Tregs), characteristically expressing CD4, CD25, and the transcription factor FoxP3, function primarily to:
options: Amplify inflammatory responses against all antigens
Suppress excessive or self-reactive immune responses, maintaining peripheral immune tolerance
Directly kill virus-infected cells
Produce large quantities of IgE
questions.correct_answer: Suppress excessive or self-reactive immune responses, maintaining peripheral immune tolerance
questions.explanation: Regulatory T cells suppress the activation and proliferation of other immune cells, playing a central role in maintaining peripheral tolerance and preventing autoimmunity.

questions.question: Central tolerance, whereby self-reactive T lymphocytes are eliminated during development, occurs primarily in the:
options: Spleen
Thymus
Bone marrow only
Lymph nodes
questions.correct_answer: Thymus
questions.explanation: Central tolerance for T cells occurs in the thymus through positive selection (for functional MHC recognition) and negative selection (deletion of strongly self-reactive T cells) during T-cell maturation.

questions.question: The complement system's classical pathway is typically initiated by:
options: Spontaneous hydrolysis of C3 in plasma
Binding of C1q to antigen-antibody (IgG or IgM) immune complexes
Direct binding of mannose-binding lectin to pathogen surface carbohydrates
Activation only by fungal cell walls
questions.correct_answer: Binding of C1q to antigen-antibody (IgG or IgM) immune complexes
questions.explanation: The classical complement pathway is initiated when C1q binds to the Fc regions of antibody (IgM or clustered IgG) already bound to antigen, triggering the C1 complex to activate C4 and C2.

questions.question: The membrane attack complex (MAC), formed by complement components C5b-C9, kills target cells primarily by:
options: Coating the pathogen to enhance phagocytosis (opsonisation) only
Forming a pore in the target cell membrane, causing osmotic lysis
Neutralising toxins directly
Activating T-cell receptors
questions.correct_answer: Forming a pore in the target cell membrane, causing osmotic lysis
questions.explanation: C5b-C9 assemble into the membrane attack complex, a transmembrane pore that disrupts osmotic balance and causes lysis of the target cell, typically Gram-negative bacteria or other pathogens.

questions.question: C3b generated during complement activation contributes importantly to immunity by acting as:
options: An opsonin that coats pathogens, enhancing phagocytosis via complement receptors on phagocytes
An antibody isotype
A cytokine that suppresses inflammation
A component of the T-cell receptor complex
questions.correct_answer: An opsonin that coats pathogens, enhancing phagocytosis via complement receptors on phagocytes
questions.explanation: C3b covalently binds pathogen surfaces and acts as a potent opsonin, being recognised by complement receptor 1 (CR1) on phagocytes, greatly enhancing phagocytic uptake and destruction of the pathogen.

questions.question: Type I hypersensitivity reactions (e.g. hay fever, anaphylaxis) are mediated by which mechanism?
options: IgE-sensitised mast cell degranulation upon allergen cross-linking of bound IgE
Deposition of antigen-antibody immune complexes in tissues
Direct cytotoxic T-cell killing of target cells
Antibody-mediated destruction of red blood cells
questions.correct_answer: IgE-sensitised mast cell degranulation upon allergen cross-linking of bound IgE
questions.explanation: Type I hypersensitivity involves allergen cross-linking IgE bound to FcεRI on mast cells/basophils, triggering rapid degranulation and release of histamine and other mediators, producing immediate allergic symptoms.

questions.question: Type II hypersensitivity reactions, such as in haemolytic disease of the newborn or autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, are mediated by:
options: IgE bound to mast cells
Antibodies (IgG/IgM) directed against antigens on the surface of specific cells, leading to complement activation or ADCC-mediated cell destruction
T-cell mediated delayed reactions occurring over 48-72 hours
Immune complex deposition in blood vessel walls
questions.correct_answer: Antibodies (IgG/IgM) directed against antigens on the surface of specific cells, leading to complement activation or ADCC-mediated cell destruction
questions.explanation: Type II hypersensitivity involves antibody binding directly to cell-surface or matrix-associated antigens, triggering complement-mediated lysis, opsonisation/phagocytosis, or antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC).

questions.question: Type III hypersensitivity reactions, such as serum sickness, are primarily caused by:
options: Deposition of soluble antigen-antibody immune complexes in tissues, triggering complement activation and inflammation
IgE cross-linking on mast cells
Direct T-cell cytotoxicity
Absence of any antibody involvement
questions.correct_answer: Deposition of soluble antigen-antibody immune complexes in tissues, triggering complement activation and inflammation
questions.explanation: Type III hypersensitivity results from deposition of circulating immune complexes (antigen-antibody) in tissues such as blood vessels, joints, and kidneys, activating complement and recruiting inflammatory cells.

questions.question: Type IV hypersensitivity (delayed-type hypersensitivity), exemplified by the tuberculin skin test, is mediated by:
options: Antibody-antigen complexes
Sensitised T lymphocytes (Th1 cells and macrophages) responding over 24-72 hours, without a primary antibody role
IgE and mast cells
Complement alone
questions.correct_answer: Sensitised T lymphocytes (Th1 cells and macrophages) responding over 24-72 hours, without a primary antibody role
questions.explanation: Type IV (delayed-type) hypersensitivity is cell-mediated, driven by antigen-specific Th1 cells that recruit and activate macrophages, producing a response that peaks 24-72 hours after antigen exposure, as in the tuberculin (Mantoux) test.

questions.question: A live attenuated vaccine (e.g. oral polio vaccine, BCG, measles vaccine) works by:
options: Using a weakened form of the pathogen that replicates poorly but stimulates strong, often long-lasting immunity similar to natural infection
Using only a chemically inactivated toxin
Providing pre-formed antibodies for passive immunity
Injecting bacterial DNA that never expresses antigen
questions.correct_answer: Using a weakened form of the pathogen that replicates poorly but stimulates strong, often long-lasting immunity similar to natural infection
questions.explanation: Live attenuated vaccines contain a pathogen weakened so it cannot cause disease in healthy individuals but still replicates enough to strongly stimulate both humoral and cell-mediated immunity, often giving durable protection.

questions.question: Passive immunity, such as administration of anti-tetanus immunoglobulin or maternal antibody transfer via the placenta, differs from active immunity in that:
options: It provides long-lasting immunological memory
It provides immediate but temporary protection, since the recipient's own immune system is not stimulated to produce memory cells
It always requires vaccination first
It only works against viral infections
questions.correct_answer: It provides immediate but temporary protection, since the recipient's own immune system is not stimulated to produce memory cells
questions.explanation: Passive immunity involves transfer of pre-formed antibodies, giving immediate protection, but because the recipient's own lymphocytes are not activated, no immunological memory is generated and protection wanes as the antibodies degrade.

questions.question: Hybridoma technology, developed by Kohler and Milstein, is used to produce monoclonal antibodies by:
options: Fusing an antibody-producing B lymphocyte with an immortal myeloma cell to create a cell line that secretes a single, defined antibody indefinitely
Extracting polyclonal antiserum directly from an immunised animal
Chemically synthesising antibodies without any cells
Cloning T lymphocytes only
questions.correct_answer: Fusing an antibody-producing B lymphocyte with an immortal myeloma cell to create a cell line that secretes a single, defined antibody indefinitely
questions.explanation: Hybridoma technology fuses a short-lived, antibody-secreting B cell with an immortal myeloma cell; the resulting hybridoma proliferates indefinitely while secreting a single monoclonal antibody of defined specificity.

questions.question: In an indirect ELISA (enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay) used to detect a patient's antibodies against a pathogen, the colour signal is generated by:
options: An enzyme-labelled secondary antibody that binds the patient's primary antibody, converting a substrate into a coloured product
Direct visualisation of the pathogen under a microscope
Agglutination of red blood cells
Radioactive decay of a labelled antigen
questions.correct_answer: An enzyme-labelled secondary antibody that binds the patient's primary antibody, converting a substrate into a coloured product
questions.explanation: In indirect ELISA, patient antibody (primary antibody) bound to plate-coated antigen is detected using an enzyme-conjugated anti-human secondary antibody; addition of substrate produces a measurable colour change proportional to antibody present.

questions.question: Primary lymphoid organs, where lymphocytes develop and mature, include the:
options: Spleen and lymph nodes
Bone marrow and thymus
Tonsils and Peyer's patches
Skin and mucosa only
questions.correct_answer: Bone marrow and thymus
questions.explanation: Bone marrow (site of B-cell and all blood cell development) and the thymus (site of T-cell maturation) are the primary lymphoid organs; the spleen and lymph nodes are secondary lymphoid organs where mature lymphocytes encounter antigen.

questions.question: Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) causes progressive immunodeficiency primarily by infecting and depleting which cell population?
options: CD8+ cytotoxic T cells
CD4+ helper T lymphocytes
Erythrocytes
Platelets
questions.correct_answer: CD4+ helper T lymphocytes
questions.explanation: HIV uses CD4 (with co-receptors CCR5/CXCR4) to enter and infect CD4+ helper T cells, progressively depleting this population and impairing the coordination of both humoral and cell-mediated immune responses, leading to AIDS.

questions.question: Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID) is a life-threatening condition characterised by:
options: Isolated deficiency of IgA only, often asymptomatic
A profound defect affecting both T-lymphocyte and B-lymphocyte function, leaving the infant vulnerable to virtually all classes of pathogens
Overproduction of all immunoglobulin classes
A purely cosmetic skin condition
questions.correct_answer: A profound defect affecting both T-lymphocyte and B-lymphocyte function, leaving the infant vulnerable to virtually all classes of pathogens
questions.explanation: SCID results from genetic defects (e.g. in cytokine receptor signalling or recombination machinery) that cripple both T- and B-cell development/function, causing severe, often fatal susceptibility to infections without treatment such as bone marrow transplant.

questions.question: In organ transplantation, hyperacute graft rejection occurs within minutes to hours because the recipient already has:
options: No immune system at all
Pre-formed antibodies against donor antigens (e.g. ABO blood group or HLA antigens) that immediately trigger complement-mediated vascular damage
A deficiency of complement proteins
Only innate immune cells, with no adaptive immunity
questions.correct_answer: Pre-formed antibodies against donor antigens (e.g. ABO blood group or HLA antigens) that immediately trigger complement-mediated vascular damage
questions.explanation: Hyperacute rejection is caused by pre-existing recipient antibodies (from prior sensitisation or ABO incompatibility) binding donor vascular endothelium immediately after transplantation, activating complement and causing rapid thrombosis and graft destruction.

questions.question: Cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CD8+) kill infected or tumour target cells primarily through which mechanism?
options: Secreting antibodies that opsonise the target
Release of perforin and granzymes that induce apoptosis in the target cell, and Fas-FasL interactions
Direct phagocytosis of the target cell
Activation of complement's alternative pathway only
questions.correct_answer: Release of perforin and granzymes that induce apoptosis in the target cell, and Fas-FasL interactions
questions.explanation: CTLs kill target cells mainly by directional release of perforin (forming pores) and granzymes (proteases that trigger apoptosis) into the immune synapse, and via Fas ligand engaging Fas on the target to induce apoptosis.

questions.question: Cytokines such as interleukin-2 (IL-2) are important in adaptive immunity mainly because they:
options: Function as structural proteins in the antibody molecule
Act as signalling molecules that regulate proliferation, differentiation, and effector functions of immune cells
Directly neutralise viral particles
Replace the need for antigen recognition
questions.correct_answer: Act as signalling molecules that regulate proliferation, differentiation, and effector functions of immune cells
questions.explanation: Cytokines like IL-2 are soluble signalling proteins that mediate communication between immune cells, driving processes such as T-cell clonal expansion (IL-2), differentiation into effector subsets, and inflammation.

questions.question: Autoimmune disease arises when immune tolerance mechanisms fail, resulting in:
options: Complete absence of any immune response
The immune system mounting a damaging response against the body's own self-antigens
Overproduction of red blood cells only
Immunity exclusively against foreign pathogens with no self-reactivity possible
questions.correct_answer: The immune system mounting a damaging response against the body's own self-antigens
questions.explanation: Autoimmune disease results from breakdown of central and/or peripheral tolerance mechanisms, allowing self-reactive lymphocytes to attack the body's own tissues, as seen in conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus.
